title: Those Viral Bodega Peptides Aren’t Actually Peptides
gist: WIRED bought $376.20 of injectable peptides (PT-141, BPC-157, NAD+, retatrutide) from a Brooklyn bodega and lab testing via Austin startup Finnrick found none contained the labeled active ingredient. The episode exposes a grey-market peptide industry investors value at up to $3 billion, built on shared shoddy upstream suppliers and 'research use only' labeling, just as the FDA loosens rules and telehealth platforms like Hims and Mochi prepare to sell peptides at scale.

insights.claim: Four injectable peptide vials bought over the counter at a Brooklyn bodega for $376.20 — PT-141, BPC-157, NAD+, and retatrutide — all failed label-claim analysis, containing none of the active ingredients printed on their labels.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Product-authenticity failure rates this total mean the consumer peptide category carries brand-destroying recall/liability risk for any listed firm that enters it.
insights.quote: The bad news: They weren’t peptides.
insights.locator: In August, the results came in.

insights.claim: The same bodega-channel vials tested low for heavy metals and endotoxins, meaning the dominant failure mode in this sample was inert 'duds' rather than acute toxicity.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Low acute-harm rates delay the body-count headlines that usually force regulatory crackdowns, extending the window in which the grey market keeps growing.
insights.locator: The (relatively) good news: The samples contained low levels of heavy metals

insights.claim: Independent label-claim testing cannot say what a failed vial actually contains — it only verifies a sample against the standard the buyer names — so negative results leave the true contents of grey-market injectables unknown.
insights.speaker: Marco Krause
insights.so_what: The testing layer sold to consumers is far weaker than it appears; a real assay/identification service is an unfilled niche in this supply chain.
insights.quote: What we offer is simply a label claim analysis. So you send us what you claim to think it is, and then we run it against a standard and verify whether or not it's the right compound
insights.locator: What did they contain? Hard to say

insights.claim: A second independent test — two retatrutide and two NAD+ vials from a smoke shop, analyzed by Texas-based Analytical Formulations — returned 'not positively identified,' corroborating that failures are not a single-lab artifact.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Two labs, two retailers, same result — treat the failure rate as a channel-wide characteristic rather than an outlier.
insights.locator: Jeff Colhoun, the founder of the research-peptide vendor directory Peptide Critic

insights.claim: Peptides degrade with temperature changes and require refrigeration, so a convenience-store distribution channel can destroy a genuine product between manufacture and sale even absent fraud.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Cold-chain integrity, not just sourcing, is the binding constraint on any legitimate at-scale peptide retail model.
insights.locator: Peptides are often sensitive to temperature changes and require refrigeration

insights.claim: A proliferation of peptide labels traces back to shared upstream vendors via 'turnkey services' that let almost anyone launch a peptide business, so one bad supplier contaminates many nominally independent brands at once.
insights.speaker: Raphaël Mazoyer
insights.so_what: Brand-level diligence is worthless here; correlated supplier risk means one enforcement action can wipe out a whole cohort of labels simultaneously.
insights.quote: There are a whole bunch of labels popping up that have the same upstream vendor
insights.locator: he points to the popularity of so-called turnkey services

insights.claim: An independent testing firm reports a rising share of dud results over the past three months, though it concedes the signal is confounded by its own growing sample volume.
insights.speaker: Raphaël Mazoyer
insights.so_what: An early, noisy leading indicator of supply-chain deterioration worth tracking before it shows up in enforcement or injury data.
insights.locator: Over the past three months, Mazoyer says, the company has seen an uptick

insights.claim: China is a major source of the peptide ingredients feeding the US grey market, and at least one importer's product was adulterated with steroids.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Import-side chokepoints (customs, API sourcing) are where any serious crackdown would land, hitting the cheapest suppliers first.
insights.locator: a man in South Bend, Indiana, was sentenced to six years in prison

insights.claim: A peptide vendor's claimed certificates of analysis were disowned by the laboratory named on them, and the vendor's website moved behind a login shortly after press contact — showing the documentation layer of this market is itself falsifiable.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Certificates of analysis cannot be used as a diligence artifact in this category; assume paperwork fraud until independently verified.
insights.locator: INDR Labs did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment

themes.theme: Market size and the coming legitimization wave

insights.claim: Investors estimate the research-peptide ecosystem is already worth up to $3 billion, according to Bloomberg News reporting, despite most of its products lacking drug approval.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: A $3B unregulated TAM is the prize drawing telehealth incumbents in — size the legitimate opportunity off this, discounted for enforcement risk.
insights.locator: this booming ecosystem that investors estimate is already worth up to $3 billion

insights.claim: Large telehealth platforms including Hims and Mochi are preparing to sell a broad array of peptides while the FDA loosens regulations, setting up a transfer of demand from bodegas and smoke shops to branded distribution.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: The formalization trade: incumbent telehealth names capture grey-market volume, but inherit the same contaminated upstream suppliers and the liability that comes with them.
insights.locator: While the FDA has taken recent steps to loosen regulations

insights.claim: Celebrity and official endorsement — including from US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and podcaster Joe Rogan — is the demand driver for peptides, not clinical evidence, which remains thin.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Demand here is influencer-driven and therefore fast-moving in both directions; it can reverse as quickly as it built.
insights.locator: Peptides have surged in popularity in recent years

insights.claim: The 'research use only' label on over-the-counter peptides is a liability shield rather than a safety statement, and gives buyers no assurance about vial contents.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Any business model resting on the research-use carve-out is one enforcement memo away from being illegal.
insights.locator: The sign at Mr. Green advertising the peptides

insights.claim: Low enforcement volume against the research-peptide industry reflects an administration view that regulation stifles innovation and that patients should choose their own products, according to a pharmaceutical regulatory compliance attorney.
insights.speaker: Darshan Kulkarni
insights.so_what: Enforcement risk is a political variable, not a legal one — it can re-rate the whole category on an administration change.
insights.quote: regulation stifles innovation, and therefore they believe that it is in the interest of patients to allow them to decide what products to take
insights.locator: Kulkarni believes that the relatively low number of enforcement actions

insights.claim: The core danger is legitimization without verification — products gain consumer acceptance while safety, accuracy, adulteration and misbranding profiles remain entirely unknown.
insights.speaker: Darshan Kulkarni
insights.so_what: The gap between perceived legitimacy and actual verification is where the tail-risk event (mass injury, class action) gets created.
insights.quote: My concern with the peptide industry is, we're legitimizing products, and we have no idea what's in them.
insights.locator: says Darshan Kulkarni, an attorney focused on pharmaceutical regulatory compliance

insights.claim: Traditional pharmacy safeguards — visual inspection, barcoding, prescription-accuracy checks — simply do not exist in convenience-store distribution, which is the structural reason the failure rate is so high.
insights.speaker: Darshan Kulkarni
insights.so_what: Channel infrastructure, not molecule quality, is the differentiator any credible entrant must buy or build.
insights.quote: Someone selling a product at a bodega doesn't know how to do that
insights.locator: In the traditional pharmaceutical sales world, steps are taken

insights.claim: A woman died this year after a peptide injection at an unlicensed medical spa in the Bronx, and a South Bend, Indiana seller of steroid-adulterated 'research use' peptides got six years in prison — evidence that real harm and real criminal exposure already exist.
insights.speaker: Sophie Kleeman
insights.so_what: Precedent for both civil harm and criminal sentencing is established; the legal machinery is in place and only needs political will to scale.
insights.locator: a woman died this year after receiving a peptide injection
